chem_ocra.10.0.summary: Groups 1, 7, and 0 of the Periodic Table show clear chemical and physical trends determined entirely by the number of electrons in their outer shells. Group 1 alkali metals become more reactive down the group as outer electrons are lost more easily, whereas Group 7 halogens become less reactive as outer electrons are gained with greater difficulty due to increased shielding and distance. Group 0 noble gases are exceptionally unreactive and stable because they possess a full outer shell of electrons.

core.h: Introduction to the Periodic Table and Outer Shells
core.p: The Periodic Table is arranged in order of **atomic number** (proton number). Elements in the same group have the same number of outer shell electrons, which explains why they share similar chemical properties.
bullets: Groups are vertical columns numbered 1 to 7, plus Group 0.
Periods are horizontal rows representing the number of electron shells.
The **outer electron shell** dictates how an element reacts and forms bonds.
Elements react to achieve a stable electronic configuration, typically a full outer shell (like a noble gas).

callouts.p: For main group elements, the group number tells you exactly how many electrons are in the outer shell.

fig.cap: Periodic table overview showing the position of Group 1 (alkali metals), Group 7 (halogens), and Group 0 (noble gases).

core.h: Group 1: Physical Properties of Alkali Metals
core.p: Group 1 elements are known as the **alkali metals**. They possess unique physical properties that set them apart from transition metals.
bullets: They are exceptionally soft and can be easily cut with a scalpel.
They have relatively low melting and boiling points, which decrease further down the group.
They have very low densities; lithium, sodium, and potassium actually float on water.
They are shiny and silvery when freshly cut, but tarnish rapidly in air as they react with oxygen.

callouts.p: Do not assume density strictly increases down Group 1; potassium is actually less dense than sodium due to atomic spacing.

core.h: Group 1: Chemical Properties and Reactions
core.p: Alkali metals are extremely reactive because they have a **single electron in their outer shell**, which they lose easily during chemical reactions to form 1+ ions.
bullets: They react vigorously with water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas.
Equation (Sodium): 2Na (s) + 2H2O (l) -> 2NaOH (aq) + H2 (g).
They react with oxygen in the air to form metal oxides (e.g., 4Na + O2 -> 2Na2O).
They react with halogens to form white ionic salt crystals.

callouts.p: Elements in Group 1 that react with water to form alkaline solutions.

core.h: Group 1: Reactivity Trend Down the Group
core.p: Reactivity in Group 1 **increases as you go down the group**. Lithium is the least reactive alkali metal, while francium is the most reactive.
bullets: Down the group, atoms get larger and have more electron shells.
The outer electron is further away from the positive nucleus, weakening the electrostatic attraction.
Inner shells shield the outer electron from the nuclear charge.
Because of increased distance and **shielding**, the outer electron is lost much more easily in lower elements.

callouts.p: Always mention: 1. More shells/larger atomic radius. 2. More shielding. 3. Weaker attraction to outer electron. 4. Electron lost more easily.

fig.cap: Atomic structure comparison showing increased shell number and shielding from lithium to potassium.

core.h: Group 7: Physical Properties of Halogens
core.p: Group 7 elements are known as the **halogens**. They are non-metals that exist as diatomic molecules (molecules made of pairs of atoms, such as Cl2).
bullets: Fluorine is a yellow gas; Chlorine is a green-yellow gas; Bromine is a red-brown liquid; Iodine is a dark grey solid.
Melting and boiling points **increase** down the group.
Fluorine has the lowest boiling point (gas), while iodine has the highest (solid at room temperature).
They are poor conductors of heat and electricity.

callouts.p: Always write halogens with a subscript 2 when referring to the element (F2, Cl2, Br2, I2).

core.h: Group 7: Chemical Properties and Reactions
core.p: Halogens have **seven electrons in their outer shell**. They react by gaining one electron to achieve a full outer shell, forming 1- ions ( halide ions) or sharing electrons in covalent bonds.
bullets: They react with metals to form metal halides (salts), e.g., 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl.
They react with hydrogen to form hydrogen halides, which dissolve in water to form acidic solutions.
Halogen atoms form single covalent bonds with each other to make diatomic molecules.
They exhibit a trend in reactivity opposite to Group 1.

callouts.p: Salt-making non-metal elements found in Group 7 of the Periodic Table.

core.h: Group 7: Reactivity Trend and Displacement Reactions
core.p: Reactivity in Group 7 **decreases down the group**. Fluorine is the most reactive halogen, and iodine is the least reactive.
bullets: Down the group, atoms get larger, outer shell electrons are further from the nucleus, and shielding increases.
It becomes harder for the atom to **attract and gain** an incoming electron.
A more reactive halogen will **displace** a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its salt.
Example: Chlorine + Potassium bromide -> Potassium chloride + Bromine (Cl2 + 2KBr -> 2KCl + Br2).

callouts.p: Halogen displacement is a redox reaction where the more reactive halogen acts as an oxidising agent by gaining electrons.

fig.cap: Halogen displacement reaction tube showing colour changes when chlorine displaces bromine or iodine.

core.h: Group 0: Physical Properties of Noble Gases
core.p: Group 0 elements are known as the **noble gases**. They are unreactive non-metals that exist as single, monatomic atoms.
bullets: Colourless gases at room temperature.
Low boiling points, which **increase** down the group as atomic size and intermolecular forces increase.
Non-flammable and safe to use in various applications.
Insoluble in water under normal conditions.

callouts.p: Unlike halogens, noble gases exist as single atoms (e.g., He, Ne) because their outer shells are already full.

core.h: Group 0: Chemical Inertness and Electronic Structure
core.p: Noble gases are exceptionally **inert** (unreactive) because they possess a **full outer shell** of electrons.
bullets: Helium has 2 electrons in its outer shell (a full first shell).
Neon, argon, krypton, and xenon have 8 electrons in their outer shell (a stable octet).
Because their outer shell is already full, they have no tendency to lose, gain, or share electrons.
They do not form molecules easily and rarely participate in chemical reactions.

callouts.p: Unreactive, stable elements in Group 0 with full outer electron shells.

core.h: Required Practical C1: Investigating Group Reactions
core.p: PAG C1 involves safely observing the reactions of Group 1 metals with water and carrying out halogen displacement reactions.
bullets: Group 1 with water: Use small pea-sized pieces of metal with safety screens and wear eye protection.
Observe effervescence (hydrogen gas), movement on water, and melting into a ball (potassium/sodium).
Test resulting solution with universal indicator (turns purple, alkaline NaOH formed).
Halogen displacement: Mix chlorine water, bromine water, and iodine solution with potassium halide salt solutions to observe colour changes.

callouts.p: Potassium reacts explosively with water; always use safety screens and small quantities during PAG C1.

analogy.t: The Musical Chairs Game of Outer Electrons
analogy.p:
Imagine a game of musical chairs where chairs represent spaces in the outer shell. Group 1 players have only one extra ticket they desperately want to give away so they can sit down and relax (full shell). Group 7 players are frantically searching for one single ticket to fill their last empty chair. Group 0 players are already comfortably seated with all chairs completely full, watching everyone else run around, completely uninterested in joining the game. 

Where it breaks down: Atoms do not have conscious desires; chemical reactions are driven entirely by electrostatic attraction, energy changes, and the pursuit of thermodynamic stability rather than a personal desire for a chair.

terms.d: An element in Group 1 of the Periodic Table that reacts with water to form an alkaline solution.
A non-metal element in Group 7 of the Periodic Table that forms salts when reacting with metals.
An unreactive, monatomic element in Group 0 of the Periodic Table with a full outer electron shell.
The repulsion of outer shell electrons by inner shell electrons, reducing the pull from the nucleus.
A chemical reaction where a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound.
Existing as molecules composed of two atoms joined by a covalent bond (e.g., Cl2).
Existing as single, unbonded atoms rather than molecules (e.g., He).
The attractive force between oppositely charged particles, such as a positive nucleus and negative electrons.
The tendency of a substance to undergo a chemical reaction.
The distance from the centre of the nucleus to the boundary of the surrounding electron shell.
A negative ion formed when a halogen gains an electron (e.g., Cl-).
Chemically unreactive.

mistakes.w: Saying reactivity decreases down Group 1 because atoms get bigger.
mistakes.r: Reactivity increases down Group 1 because the outer electron is further away and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.

mistakes.w: Writing halogen elements as single atoms like Cl or Br without the subscript 2.
mistakes.r: Halogens exist as diatomic molecules in their elemental state: Cl2, Br2, I2, F2.

mistakes.w: Stating Group 0 elements are diatomic.
mistakes.r: Group 0 elements are monatomic (single atoms: He, Ne, Ar).

mistakes.w: Explaining Group 7 trends by saying they lose electrons.
mistakes.r: Halogens react by gaining an electron (or sharing one) to fill their outer shell.

mistakes.w: Confusing halide ions with halogen atoms (e.g., chloride vs chlorine).
mistakes.r: Chlorine is the element (Cl2); chloride is the ion formed when it gains an electron (Cl-).

mistakes.w: Forgetting safety precautions in Group 1 practicals.
mistakes.r: Must mention safety glasses, safety screens, and small quantities.

mistakes.w: Stating that noble gases have zero electrons in their outer shell.
mistakes.r: Noble gases have a full outer shell (2 for helium, 8 for others).

exam.q: Explain why potassium is more reactive than lithium in Group 1.
model: Potassium has more electron shells / larger atomic radius than lithium.
The outer electron in potassium is further from the nucleus and experiences more shielding from inner shells.
Therefore, the electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron is weaker, so the electron is lost more easily.
exam.tip: Always link atomic size, shielding, and electrostatic attraction in Group 1 explanations.

exam.q: State the colour and physical state of bromine at room temperature.
model: Colour: Red-brown
State: Liquid
exam.tip: Memorise states and colours for all four main halogens (F, Cl, Br, I).

exam.q: Explain why noble gases are unreactive.
model: They have a full outer shell of electrons.
Therefore, they have no tendency to lose, gain, or share electrons.
exam.tip: Keep it concise: full outer shell = no need to react.

exam.q: Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction of sodium with water.
model: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2
Correct state symbols: (s), (l), (aq), (g) (if required).
exam.tip: Remember water is H2O and sodium hydroxide is NaOH.

exam.q: Describe what you would observe when chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution.
model: Solution turns brown / darkens.
Because iodine is displaced.
Iodine is formed in the solution.
exam.tip: Mention both the colour change and the substance displaced.

exam.q: Explain the trend in reactivity down Group 7.
model: Reactivity decreases down Group 7.
Atoms get larger with more electron shells.
Outer shell is further from the nucleus and experiences more shielding.
It is harder to attract and gain an incoming electron.
exam.tip: Contrast this carefully with Group 1 where electrons are lost.

exam.q: Give two physical properties of Group 1 metals that make them different from transition metals.
model: Lower melting points.
Lower densities (can float on water).
exam.tip: Do not use properties shared by all metals like electrical conductivity.

exam.q: Explain why fluorine is a gas at room temperature while iodine is a solid.
model: Melting and boiling points increase down Group 7.
Fluorine has a low boiling point below room temperature, whereas iodine has a higher melting/boiling point above room temp.
exam.tip: Link state to the trend in boiling points.

exam.q: State what is formed when a halogen reacts with a metal.
model: A metal halide / salt.
exam.tip: Keep direct recall questions brief and precise.

worked.q: Predict whether a displacement reaction will occur when bromine water is added to sodium chloride solution, and explain why.
steps: Identify the reactivity of the halogen added (bromine) and the halogen in the salt (chlorine).
Recall the reactivity trend of Group 7 (reactivity decreases down the group: fluorine > chlorine > bromine > iodine).
Compare positions: chlorine is above bromine, meaning chlorine is more reactive than bromine.
Conclude whether displacement occurs: bromine cannot displace chlorine from sodium chloride.
worked.ans: No reaction occurs because bromine is less reactive than chlorine and cannot displace it from its salt solution.

worked.q: Calculate the mass of hydrogen gas produced when 4.6 g of sodium reacts completely with excess water. (Relative atomic masses: Na = 23, H = 1)
steps: Write the balanced equation: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2
Calculate moles of sodium: Moles = Mass / Ar = 4.6 / 23 = 0.2 moles.
Use molar ratio from equation: 2 moles of Na produce 1 mole of H2. Therefore, 0.2 moles of Na produce 0.2 / 2 = 0.1 moles of H2.
Calculate mass of hydrogen: Mass = Moles x Mr = 0.1 x 2 = 0.2 g.
worked.ans: 0.2 g of hydrogen gas is produced.

chem_ocra.10.1.summary: Transition metals are d-block elements located in the central block of the Periodic Table between Groups 2 and 3. Unlike Group 1 alkali metals, transition metals are hard, dense, strong, and have much higher melting points, yet they are significantly less reactive. A defining chemical characteristic of transition metals is their ability to form coloured compounds, act as industrial catalysts, and exhibit multiple oxidation states with variable valency.

core.h: Position and Physical Properties of Transition Metals
core.p: Transition metals occupy the central rectangular block of the Periodic Table between Group 2 and Group 3. Physically, they contrast sharply with the soft, highly reactive Group 1 alkali metals by being dense, hard, strong, and possessing exceptionally high melting and boiling points.
bullets: Located in periods 4, 5 and 6 between Group 2 and Group 3.
High melting and boiling points compared to Group 1 metals.
High density and mechanical strength, making them useful for structural engineering.
Good conductors of heat and electricity in both solid and liquid states.

head: Property
Group 1 (Alkali Metals)
Transition Metals (e.g., Iron, Copper)
rows: Soft (can be cut with a knife)

core.h: Comparison with Group 1 Metals
core.p: While both groups consist of metals that lose electrons to form positive ions, their chemical and physical behaviours are entirely different. Group 1 metals react violently with water and oxygen at room temperature, whereas transition metals do not react quickly with water or air.
bullets: Group 1 elements are much more reactive than transition metals.
Transition metals react slowly or not at all with cold water and oxygen.
Iron requires both oxygen and water over a long period to rust.
Transition metals do not have a single fixed oxidation state like Group 1 (+1).

callouts.p: Reactivity decreases across the transition series, making them vastly more stable and corrosion-resistant than alkali metals.

core.h: Variable Oxidation States and Valencies
core.p: Unlike Group 1 elements which only form +1 ions, transition metals can form ions with different charges (oxidation states). This is because electrons from inner d-orbitals can be lost alongside outer s-electrons during chemical reactions.
bullets: Iron forms iron(II) ions (Fe2+) and iron(III) ions (Fe3+).
Copper forms copper(I) ions (Cu+) and copper(II) ions (Cu2+).
Different oxidation states result in different chemical properties and colours.
Roman numerals in IUPAC names indicate the specific oxidation state of the metal.

callouts.p: The ability of an element to combine in more than one ratio by exhibiting multiple positive oxidation states.

core.h: Formation of Coloured Compounds
core.p: A hallmark of transition metal chemistry is that their solid compounds and aqueous solutions are vividly coloured. These colours depend on the specific transition metal ion and its oxidation state.
bullets: Copper(II) sulfate solution is blue.
Iron(II) compounds (like iron(II) sulfate) are pale green.
Iron(III) compounds (like iron(III) chloride) are orange-brown.
Nickel(II) compounds are typically green.

core.h: Catalytic Properties of Transition Metals
core.p: Transition metals and their compounds are widely used as catalysts in industrial chemical processes. A catalyst speeds up a chemical rate without being chemically changed or used up at the end of the reaction.
bullets: Iron is used as a catalyst in the Haber process to manufacture ammonia.
Nickel is used to hydrogenate alkenes to make margarine.
Platinum and rhodium are used in catalytic converters in car exhausts.
Manganese(IV) oxide catalyses the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.

callouts.p: Transition metal catalysts lower activation energy, saving millions of pounds in industrial energy costs.

core.h: Transition Metals as Catalysts: Mechanism
core.p: Transition metals make effective catalysts because they can easily give away and accept electrons, or temporarily form intermediate bonds with reactant molecules due to vacant orbitals in their d-subshells.
bullets: Provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
Reactants temporarily adsorb onto the surface of the transition metal catalyst.
Bonds within reactant molecules weaken, making them react faster.
Products desorb from the catalyst surface, leaving the metal unchanged.

callouts.p: Always state that a catalyst is **not used up** during the reaction and remains chemically unchanged at the end.

core.h: Iron in the Haber Process
core.p: The Haber process is used to manufacture ammonia for fertilizers. Nitrogen gas from the air and hydrogen gas from natural gas are passed over an **iron catalyst** at 450 degrees Celsius and 200 atmospheres pressure.
bullets: Word equation: Nitrogen + Hydrogen <=> Ammonia.
Symbol equation: N2 (g) + 3H2 (g) <=> 2NH3 (g).
Finely divided iron powder is used to maximize the surface area.
Without the iron catalyst, the reaction would be far too slow at industrial temperatures.

callouts.p: Do not write that the iron catalyst 'reacts' to form ammonia; it only speeds up the reaction rate.

core.h: Nickel in Hydrogenation
core.p: Nickel is used as a catalyst when converting unsaturated vegetable oils into saturated fats (margarine) by reacting them with hydrogen gas at around 60 degrees Celsius.
bullets: Adds hydrogen across carbon-carbon double bonds in alkenes.
Turns liquid oils into spreadable solid fats.
Nickel catalyst is filtered out and recycled after the reaction.
Essential process in the food manufacturing industry.

core.h: Precipitation Reactions of Transition Metal Ions
core.p: Aqueous transition metal ions react with sodium hydroxide solution to form distinct, coloured hydroxide precipitates. This is a key analytical test used to identify which transition metal ion is present in a solution.
bullets: Copper(II) ions give a **blue precipitate** of copper(II) hydroxide.
Iron(II) ions give a **green precipitate** of iron(II) hydroxide.
Iron(III) ions give a **brown precipitate** of iron(III) hydroxide.
Precipitates are insoluble solids suspended in the mixture.

callouts.p: An insoluble solid formed when two clear solutions react together.

core.h: Ionic Equations for Transition Metal Precipitates
core.p: When sodium hydroxide is added to transition metal salt solutions, hydroxide ions (OH-) react with the metal ions (M2+ or M3+) to form solid metal hydroxides. You must be able to write ionic equations for these reactions.
bullets: Cu2+ (aq) + 2OH- (aq) -> Cu(OH)2 (s) [Blue precipitate].
Fe2+ (aq) + 2OH- (aq) -> Fe(OH)2 (s) [Green precipitate].
Fe3+ (aq) + 3OH- (aq) -> Fe(OH)3 (s) [Brown precipitate].
Always include correct state symbols: (aq) for aqueous ions, (s) for solid precipitates.

core.h: Corrosion and Uses of Transition Metals
core.p: Transition metals are widely used in everyday life due to their high tensile strength and durability. However, iron and steel undergo corrosion (rusting) in the presence of oxygen and water, forming hydrated iron(III) oxide.
bullets: Transition metals are malleable and ductile, making them ideal for tools, bridges, and wires.
Pure iron is relatively soft, so it is alloyed with carbon and other metals to make strong steels.
Copper is used for electrical wiring because it is a brilliant conductor and does not react with water.
Titanium is used in aerospace and medical replacements because it is strong, lightweight, and corrosion-resistant.

callouts.p: Iron only rusts when both oxygen AND water are present; salt speeds up this electrochemical process.

analogy.p: Think of transition metals as the Swiss Army knives of the Periodic Table. Unlike Group 1 metals which are like single-use plastic tools (soft, reactive, and only good for one simple job), transition metals are sturdy, adaptable, change colour in different situations, and possess special attachments (catalytic abilities) to help other reactions happen faster. However, this analogy breaks down because Swiss Army knives are mechanical tools made of parts, whereas transition metal versatility stems from atomic electron arrangements in d-orbitals.

terms.p: A metal in the central block of the Periodic Table (d-block) that has high melting points, high densities, forms coloured compounds, and acts as a catalyst.
terms.d: A d-block element that forms one or more stable ions with incompletely filled d orbitals, characterized by high density, high melting point, and catalytic activity.

terms.p: A substance that speeds up the rate of a chemical reaction without being used up or chemically changed itself.
terms.d: A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.

terms.p: A number representing the charge an atom would have if ionic bonds were completely formed.
terms.d: A measure of the degree of oxidation of an atom in a substance, often indicated by Roman numerals.

terms.p: An insoluble solid formed by the reaction of two solutions.
terms.d: An insoluble solid that emerges from a liquid solution during a chemical reaction.

terms.p: The addition of hydrogen across carbon-carbon double bonds in alkenes, usually using a nickel catalyst.
terms.d: A chemical reaction between molecular hydrogen and another compound or element, typically in the presence of a catalyst.

terms.p: The industrial manufacture of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen using an iron catalyst.
terms.d: An industrial process for producing ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen using an iron catalyst at high temperature and pressure.

terms.p: The ability of an element to exhibit more than one combining power or oxidation state.
terms.d: The property of having multiple possible positive oxidation numbers in chemical compounds.

terms.p: The central section of the Periodic Table containing transition elements.
terms.d: The block of elements in groups 3 to 12 of the Periodic Table.
The chemical compound formed when iron corrodes in the presence of oxygen and water (Fe2O3.xH2O).

terms.p: An ion or molecule that binds to a central transition metal ion to form a complex.
terms.d: A Lewis base that donates a pair of electrons to a metal atom or ion to form a coordination complex.

terms.p: Capable of being hammered or pressed into shape without breaking.
terms.d: A physical property describing a material's ability to deform under compressive stress.

terms.p: Able to be drawn out into a thin wire.
terms.d: A physical property describing a material's ability to be stretched into a wire.

mistakes.w: Saying transition metals react vigorously with water like Group 1 metals.
mistakes.r: Transition metals are unreactive or react extremely slowly with water.

mistakes.w: Stating that a catalyst is used up during a chemical reaction.
mistakes.r: A catalyst remains chemically unchanged and is not used up at the end of the reaction.

mistakes.w: Describing transition metal compounds as all being white or colourless.
mistakes.r: Transition metal compounds are characteristically brightly coloured (e.g., blue copper, green iron(II)).

mistakes.w: Writing that iron is the catalyst in the hydrogenation of oils.
mistakes.r: Nickel is the catalyst used for hydrogenation; iron is used in the Haber process.

mistakes.w: Forgetting state symbols in ionic precipitation equations.
mistakes.r: Always include (aq) for aqueous ions and (s) for the solid precipitate (e.g., Cu(OH)2 (s)).

mistakes.w: Confusing iron(II) and iron(III) precipitate colours.
mistakes.r: Iron(II) gives a green precipitate, whereas iron(III) gives a brown/orange precipitate.

mistakes.w: Calling transition metals soft and low-density.
mistakes.r: Transition metals are hard, dense, strong, and have high melting points.

exam.q: Give two physical properties of transition metals that distinguish them from Group 1 metals.
model: Higher melting points (1)
Higher density / harder / stronger (1)
exam.tip: Mention two distinct physical differences. Do not talk about reactivity unless asked.

exam.q: State the catalyst used in the Haber process and give its purpose.
model: Iron (1)
To speed up the reaction rate / provide a lower activation energy pathway (1)
exam.tip: Name the metal clearly and state its function.

exam.q: Explain why transition metals are suitable for making water pipes and bridges compared to sodium.
model: Transition metals are strong and hard (1)
Sodium is soft and easily cut (1)
Transition metals have high melting points and do not react with water (1)
Sodium reacts violently with water and melts (1)
exam.tip: Contrast both materials directly using comparative language.

exam.q: A solution contains iron(II) ions. Describe what you would see when excess sodium hydroxide solution is added.
model: A green precipitate forms (1)
The precipitate is insoluble in excess sodium hydroxide (1)
exam.tip: Always state both the colour and the word 'precipitate'.

exam.q: Write the ionic equation for the formation of the precipitate when sodium hydroxide is added to copper(II) sulfate solution.
model: Cu2+ (aq) + 2OH- (aq) -> Cu(OH)2 (s) (2)
Award (1) for correct formulas and (1) for correct state symbols
exam.tip: Ensure charges balance and state symbols are included.

exam.q: Describe how transition metals differ from Group 1 elements in terms of their oxidation states and the colours of their compounds.
model: Transition metals have variable oxidation states / form ions with different charges (1)
Group 1 metals only form +1 ions (1)
Transition metal compounds are brightly coloured (1)
Group 1 compounds are white solids / colourless solutions (1)
exam.tip: Give two distinct differences: one for oxidation states and one for colour.

exam.q: Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction.
model: Provides an alternative reaction pathway (1)
Lowers the activation energy (1)
exam.tip: Learn these exact mark-scheme phrases word for word.

exam.q: State the transition metal catalyst used to convert vegetable oils into margarine.
model: Nickel / Ni (1)
exam.tip: Check whether the question asks for the name or symbol; both are usually accepted.

exam.q: Explain why iron(III) chloride solution is orange-brown while copper(II) sulfate solution is blue.
model: Different transition metal ions produce different characteristic colours (1)
Iron(III) ions give orange-brown and copper(II) ions give blue (1)
exam.tip: Link the specific ion directly to its specific colour.

worked.q: A student adds sodium hydroxide solution to an unknown transition metal solution 'X'. A brown precipitate forms. Identify metal ion X and write the balanced ionic equation for the reaction.
steps: Step 1: Recall the precipitate colours for transition metal ions: copper(II) is blue, iron(II) is green, and iron(III) is brown.
Step 2: Identify the metal ion based on the brown precipitate as iron(III) (Fe3+).
Step 3: Write the formula of the reacting aqueous ions: Fe3+ (aq) and OH- (aq).
Step 4: Balance the charges to write the formula of the solid precipitate: iron(III) hydroxide is Fe(OH)3 (s).
Step 5: Balance the ionic equation by putting a 3 in front of OH- (aq).
worked.ans: Metal ion X is Fe3+ (iron(III)). Ionic equation: Fe3+ (aq) + 3OH- (aq) -> Fe(OH)3 (s).

worked.q: Compare three physical and chemical properties of copper with those of potassium.
steps: Step 1: Identify potassium as a Group 1 alkali metal and copper as a transition metal.
Step 2: Compare melting points (Potassium is low, copper is very high).
Step 3: Compare hardness and strength (Potassium is soft and cut with a knife, copper is hard and strong).
Step 4: Compare reactivity with water (Potassium reacts violently, copper does not react with water).
worked.ans: 1. Melting point: Potassium has a low melting point, whereas copper has a very high melting point. 2. Hardness: Potassium is soft and easily cut with a knife, whereas copper is hard, strong, and rigid. 3. Reactivity: Potassium reacts vigorously and exothermically with water, whereas copper is completely unreactive with water.

chem_ocra.10.3.summary: These revision notes explore how metals react with water and dilute acids, allowing us to deduce an empirical reactivity order. By observing the rate of bubbling, temperature changes, and whether a metal reacts at all, we can place elements into a precise series. This core chemistry concept links atomic structure, specifically electron loss, directly to macroscopic observable behaviors during chemical reactions.

core.h: Reactivity Series Principles
core.p: The reactivity series arranges metals in order of their reactivity from most reactive to least reactive. This order is determined by how easily a metal atom loses its outer shell electrons to form positive ions.
bullets: More reactive metals lose their outer electrons more easily.
Metals above hydrogen in the series react with dilute acids.
Very reactive metals react with cold water; moderately reactive ones react with steam.
Unreactive metals like gold and platinum do not react with water or acids.

callouts.p: Reactivity is all about oxidation: the ease with which a metal atom forms a positive ion by losing electrons.
Although non-metals, carbon and hydrogen are included in the reactivity series as reference points for extraction and acid reactions.

core.h: Reaction of Group 1 Metals with Water
core.p: Group 1 metals (potassium, sodium, lithium) react vigorously with cold water to produce a metal hydroxide solution and hydrogen gas. The reaction gets increasingly violent down the group.
bullets: Lithium: Fizzes steadily, moves around on the surface, eventually disappears.
Sodium: Melts into a silver ball, fizzes rapidly, darts across the surface.
Potassium: Lilac flame produced, melts, reacts violently and immediately.
General equation: Metal + Water -> Metal Hydroxide + Hydrogen

callouts.p: Potassium reacts so vigorously with water that it often catches fire and spits, requiring safety screens.

core.h: Reaction of Group 2 Metals with Water
core.p: Group 2 metals show differing reactivities with water. Calcium reacts steadily with cold water, while magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water, but vigorously with steam.
bullets: Calcium + Water -> Calcium Hydroxide + Hydrogen
Magnesium + Steam -> Magnesium Oxide + Hydrogen
Calcium forms a cloudy white suspension of calcium hydroxide.
Magnesium ribbon glows brightly when reacted with steam.

callouts.p: Magnesium reacts extremely slowly with cold water because the magnesium hydroxide formed is sparingly soluble and coats the metal, slowing the reaction.

core.h: Reaction of Metals with Dilute Acids
core.p: Metals that are more reactive than hydrogen will react with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid to produce a salt and hydrogen gas. The rate of bubble production indicates reactivity.
bullets: Magnesium reacts extremely fast with lots of fizzing and heat given off.
Zinc reacts at a moderate, steady rate.
Iron reacts slowly, producing bubbles of hydrogen over time.
Copper, silver, and gold show no bubbles or temperature change with dilute acid.

callouts.p: Effervescence (bubbling) and temperature increase are key signs of a exothermic reaction between a metal and an acid.

core.h: Chemical Equations for Acid Reactions
core.p: Writing balanced symbol equations for metal-acid reactions requires knowing the valency of metal ions and the charges on common acid anions.
bullets: Magnesium + Hydrochloric Acid -> Magnesium Chloride + Hydrogen
Mg (s) + 2HCl (aq) -> MgCl2 (aq) + H2 (g)
Zinc + Sulfuric Acid -> Zinc Sulfate + Hydrogen
Zn (s) + H2SO4 (aq) -> ZnSO4 (aq) + H2 (g)

callouts.p: Hydrochloric acid produces chloride salts; sulfuric acid produces sulfate salts.

core.h: Required Practical C1: Investigating Reactivity
core.p: PAG C1 involves measuring temperature changes or observation rates when various metals react with dilute hydrochloric acid to deduce a reactivity order.
bullets: Keep the volume and concentration of acid constant using a volumetric pipette.
Use the same mass and surface area of each metal powder or ribbon.
Measure the initial and highest temperature reached using a digital thermometer.
Record observations such as rate of fizzing and time taken for the metal to disappear.

callouts.p: Surface area is critical: powdered metals react much faster than large chunks due to greater exposed surface area.

core.h: Deducing Reactivity Order from Experimental Data
core.p: Experimental results allow scientists to rank metals. The greater the temperature change or the faster the gas evolution, the more reactive the metal is.
bullets: Largest temperature rise = Most reactive metal in the test set.
No temperature change and no bubbles = Less reactive than hydrogen.
Displacement reactions can further refine the order between similar metals.
Consistency across multiple tests ensures reliable ranking.

core.h: Displacement Reactions as Confirmation
core.p: A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from a solution of its compound. This confirms the relative positions found by acid and water tests.
bullets: Magnesium + Copper Sulfate -> Magnesium Sulfate + Copper
Observation: Blue solution fades, pink-brown solid coats the magnesium.
Ionic equation: Mg (s) + Cu2+ (aq) -> Mg2+ (aq) + Cu (s)
Unreactive metals cannot displace anything from solution.

callouts.p: Displacement is a redox reaction: the metal atoms are oxidized (lose electrons) and metal ions are reduced (gain electrons).

core.h: The Role of Hydrogen in the Series
core.p: Hydrogen acts as the dividing line in the reactivity series. Metals above hydrogen react with dilute acids; metals below hydrogen do not.
bullets: Position determines whether acids can be used to generate hydrogen gas.
Acids contain hydrogen ions (H+); reactive metals force these ions to accept electrons and form H2 gas.
Unreactive metals lack the chemical push to transfer electrons to hydrogen ions.
Copper and silver sit below hydrogen and are termed noble metals in this context.

core.h: Oxidation and Reduction in Metal Reactions
core.p: In terms of electrons, reactivity is defined by how easily oxidation occurs. When a metal reacts with water or acid, it undergoes oxidation.
bullets: Oxidation is Loss of electrons (OIL).
Reduction is Gain of electrons (RIG).
Metal atoms lose electrons to form positive ions: M -> M^n+ + ne-
Hydrogen ions gain electrons to form atoms and pair up into gas: 2H+ + 2e- -> H2

callouts.p: Half equations explicitly show the electron transfer occurring during these redox reactions.

core.h: Safety and Precautions in Practical Work
core.p: Working with acids, reactive metals, and hydrogen gas requires strict adherence to laboratory safety protocols.
bullets: Wear eye protection (goggles) at all times during acid and metal experiments.
Use small pieces of Group 1 metals with safety screens due to explosion risks.
Keep naked flames away when testing for hydrogen gas.
Ensure proper ventilation when handling concentrated or hot acids.

callouts.p: To identify hydrogen gas, hold a burning splint at the mouth of the test tube; it produces a characteristic 'squeaky pop'.

analogy.p: Imagine a queue for a rollercoaster where eager, energetic people (reactive metals) push straight to the front and grab seats immediately, while lazy people (unreactive metals) refuse to move from the back. Acids and water are like the ride operators inviting people on. Where it breaks down is that human impatience varies by mood, whereas chemical reactivity is a fixed physical property determined strictly by atomic structure.

terms.d: A list of metals arranged in order of their decreasing reactivity.
A reaction where a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound.
Loss of electrons, or gain of oxygen, during a chemical reaction.
Gain of electrons, or loss of oxygen, during a chemical reaction.
Bubbling caused by the production of a gas during a chemical reaction.
A compound formed when hydrogen in an acid is replaced by a metal.
Dissolved in water.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, usually increasing temperature.
The combining power of an element, related to the charge on its ion.
An equation that shows how many electrons are lost or gained by a species during a reaction.
A metal that resists corrosion and oxidation, such as gold or platinum.
An alkaline compound containing the OH- ion.

mistakes.w: Metals react with acids to produce water and a salt.
mistakes.r: Metals react with acids to produce hydrogen gas and a salt.

mistakes.w: Copper reacts slowly with dilute hydrochloric acid.
mistakes.r: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series and does not react with dilute acid at all.

mistakes.w: Reactivity decreases as you go down Group 1.
mistakes.r: Reactivity increases down Group 1 because outer electrons are further from the nucleus and lost more easily.

mistakes.w: Magnesium reacts vigorously with cold water.
mistakes.r: Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water, but vigorously with steam.

mistakes.w: Displacement is when two metals swap places completely.
mistakes.r: Displacement is when a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal ion in solution or compound.

mistakes.w: Reduction is the loss of electrons.
mistakes.r: Reduction is the gain of electrons (RIG - Reduction Is Gain).

mistakes.w: All metals react with water to form oxides.
mistakes.r: Reactive metals form metal hydroxides with cold water, and some form oxides with steam.

exam.q: State two observations you would see when a small piece of potassium is added to cold water.
model: Fizzes / bubbles of gas produced
Lilac flame seen
Moves around on the surface / melts into a ball
exam.tip: Give distinct, observable physical changes, not just 'it reacts'.

exam.q: Explain why copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid.
model: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen
Therefore it cannot displace hydrogen from the acid
exam.tip: Always reference the position of the metal relative to hydrogen.

exam.q: Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction between magnesium and sulfuric acid.
model: Mg + H2SO4 -> MgSO4 + H2
Correct state symbols if requested (s, aq, g)
exam.tip: Check formula charges: Mg2+ and SO4 2- make MgSO4.

exam.q: Describe how a student could use magnesium, zinc, and iron to deduce their relative reactivities using dilute hydrochloric acid.
model: Add equal masses of each metal to equal volumes of hydrochloric acid of the same concentration
Measure the temperature change using a thermometer
Observe the rate of effervescence / bubbling
Magnesium will show the largest temperature change and fastest bubbling, followed by zinc, then iron
exam.tip: Mention controlling variables such as volume and concentration of acid.

exam.q: Define oxidation in terms of electrons.
model: Loss of electrons
exam.tip: Learn OIL RIG word for word to secure this mark.

exam.q: A student added zinc to copper sulfate solution. State two observations.
model: Blue solution fades / turns colourless
Pink-brown solid coats the zinc / forms in the solution
exam.tip: Remember copper metal is pink-brown, not red.

exam.q: Write the ionic equation for the displacement of copper by magnesium.
model: Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu
Correct balancing and charge symbols included
exam.tip: Omit spectator ions (like sulfate) to get the ionic equation.

exam.q: Explain why calcium reacts faster with water than magnesium does.
model: Calcium is further down Group 2 / more reactive than magnesium
Calcium loses its outer electrons more easily
exam.tip: Link group position directly to electron loss.

exam.q: Give the test and positive result for hydrogen gas.
model: Test: Hold a burning splint near the gas
Result: Squeaky pop sound
exam.tip: State both the action and the exact sound.

exam.q: Explain why oxide coatings on aluminium can make it appear unreactive in certain tests.
model: Aluminium reacts with oxygen to form a protective layer of aluminium oxide
This physical barrier prevents the acid or water from reaching the metal underneath
exam.tip: This explains why aluminium reacts slowly at first with acids.

worked.q: Calculate the mass of hydrogen gas produced when 4.8 g of magnesium reacts completely with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. (Ar of Mg = 24, H = 1)
steps: Step 1: Write the balanced symbol equation: Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2
Step 2: Calculate moles of magnesium: Moles = Mass / Ar = 4.8 / 24 = 0.2 mol
Step 3: Use the molar ratio from equation (1:1): Moles of H2 = 0.2 mol
Step 4: Calculate mass of hydrogen: Mass = Moles * Mr = 0.2 * 2 = 0.4 g

worked.q: A student tests three mystery metals (X, Y, Z) with water and acid. X reacts with cold water. Y does not react with water, but reacts rapidly with dilute acid. Z does not react with acid at all. Place them in order of reactivity from most to least reactive.
steps: Step 1: Analyse X - reacts with cold water, making it the most reactive (Group 1 or reactive Group 2).
Step 2: Analyse Y - does not react with water, but reacts rapidly with acid, placing it above hydrogen.
Step 3: Analyse Z - does not react with acid, placing it below hydrogen.
Step 4: Combine into final order from most to least reactive: X, Y, Z.
